title: The Mouse in the Dark Night
summary: A mouse roams in the dark night, eats nectar, tears existence apart, digs holes and ruins the stores; black yet without colour, it rises into the sky to graze and leaps about until the true guru's teaching makes it still, while the refrain tells the yogi to kill it so that coming and going is cut off, and Bhusuku says that when its roaming is cut off the bonds break. Munidatta reads the mouse, 'the stealer', as the mind-wind and the night as wisdom or the action-woman. In his reading the restless mind-mouse tears apart one's own body and brings about the fall into the bad destinies until the true guru's word stills it, and when its movement is cut off the bond of saṃsāra bursts.

lines.gloss: rāga, melody · Varāḍī (name of the rāga)

flags.note: The poet's name is not in the heading line itself. It comes from the attribution bhusukupādānām ('of Bhusukupāda') written before the song, which Shastri's text runs into line 1a (removed there as not part of the verse). The Tibetan heading also names him, as 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs.

lines.gloss: in the night · dark · susāra (doubtful; read musāra, of the mouse) · roaming, going about
lines.en: In the dark [night]{night} the [mouse]{mouse} goes roaming;

flags.note: Shastri marks susāra as doubtful (?), and it gives no clear sense. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the mouse here: mtshan mo mun par byi ba rgyu byed cing, 'in the dark night the mouse roams, and'. I read musāra, 'the mouse's' (genitive -ra), supposing a copying slip of s for m, and take cārā as 'roaming, going about' (car-, 'move, graze'; compare caraa in 4b and cā in 6a): 'the mouse's roaming', so 'the mouse goes roaming'. The mouse markup sits on the emended word. If susāra stands, the line has no subject until 1b ('in the dark night it goes about ...') and susāra is left unexplained (su-, 'well', with a form of sṛ-, 'move', is a guess). Munidatta quotes only the first two words, niśi āndhīrī (cp.21.m2), so he does not settle it.

lines.gloss: nectar · eats · mouse · makes · meal, food
lines.en: the [mouse]{mouse} eats [nectar]{amrta} and makes a meal of it.

lines.gloss: kill! (māra + re, hey) · yogi (vocative) · mouse · wind

flags.note: musā pabaṇā is taken as apposition, 'the mouse, the wind', following the word order. The Tibetan makes one compound of it, rlung byi, 'wind-mouse'; 'the mouse and the wind' is also possible grammatically. Munidatta treats the mouse as the mind-wind, cittapavana (cp.21.m2), but 'wind' here is the song's own word (pabaṇā), not his gloss.

The Tibetan refrain has negatives the Bengali lacks: kye'i rnal 'byor rlung byi ma bsad cing / gang gis 'gro dang 'ong ba ma bkag na, 'O yogin, not killing the wind-mouse, if coming and going is not stopped by it', a warning where the Bengali gives a command (māra re, 'kill!'). The Bengali is translated as it stands.

lines.gloss: by which, so that · breaks off, is cut off · coming · going
lines.en: so that [coming and going]{coming-and-going} is cut off.

flags.note: jem̐ṇa, the instrumental of the relative ('by which'), is taken as 'so that'. tuṭaa, 'breaks off, is cut off' (Sanskrit truṭyati, the verb Munidatta uses at cp.21.m2 and cp.21.m6), comes back in 6a and is rendered the same way. The Tibetan has the negative ma bkag, 'is not stopped' (see 2a).

lines.gloss: existence · tears apart, splits · mouse · digs · hole(s)

flags.note: Where the Bengali has the mouse dig holes (khaṇaa gātī), the Tibetan line has it bore through a wall: srid pa rnam 'joms byi bas rtsig pa 'bugs, 'destroying existence, the mouse bores through the wall'. Munidatta cites the word as gatī and takes it as gati, 'destiny', the fall into the bad destinies (cp.21.m3). 'Holes' follows the Bengali (compare Sanskrit garta, 'pit').
bindāraa, 'tears apart, splits open' (Sanskrit vidārayati, the word of Munidatta's gloss, cp.21.m3); the Tibetan has rnam 'joms, 'destroys'.

lines.gloss: restless · mouse · having looked over, having reckoned (?) · destroying, destroyer · store, what is laid by (?)
lines.en: the restless [mouse]{mouse} looks over the stores and destroys them.

flags.note: kaliām̐ is uncertain. I take it as a participle of kal-, 'observe, reckon' ('having looked over'), because Munidatta's comment on this couplet has ākalayya, 'having reckoned', and the Tibetan comment bgrangs nas, 'having counted' (cp.21.m3), though he applies the word to the yogin. Other possibilities: a form of kar-, 'do', with the eastern l for r ('wreaks ruin on the stores'); or a form of kāla, 'black' (compare kalā in 4a). thātī is taken as 'store, what is laid by' (compare Hindi thātī, 'deposit'); the Tibetan has snod rnams, 'vessels'. nāśaka, 'destroyer', is rendered as a verb.

The Tibetan line reads g.yo ba'i byi bas snod rnams ba zhing 'joms, 'the restless mouse ... and destroys the vessels'. ba zhing is unclear, perhaps corrupt, and nothing in the Tibetan clearly answers to kaliām̐.

lines.gloss: black (kāla; or: Kāla, time, death) · mouse · lacking (?) · colour (varṇa)

flags.note: kalā is rendered 'black' (kāla, with a short vowel). The Tibetan comment quotes the word as nag po, 'black'; a black mouse suits the dark night of 1a and makes a paradox with 'has no colour'. Munidatta quotes it as kāla and says the mind-mouse is kāla because it destroys conventional bodhicitta (cp.21.m4), that is, kāla as 'time, death', the destroyer (the glossary's kala, 'Death'). The word carries both senses; the alternative line is 'Death, the mouse, has no colour'. The glossary did not detect কলা as kala; see termsOmitted.

uhaṇa bāṇa: 'has no colour' rests on the two old readings. Munidatta takes bāṇa as varṇa, 'colour', saying that when the mouse is examined no colour is found to apprehend (cp.21.m4), and the Tibetan line has kha dog med, 'without colour'. Taking uhaṇa as 'lacking' (compare Sanskrit ūna, 'wanting', or Apabhraṃśa vihūṇa, 'without') is my conjecture.

The Tibetan line is byi ba sgra gcan spu dang kha dog med, 'the mouse, Rāhu, has no fur and no colour'. It puts the commentary's gloss, Rāhu (sgra gcan), into the verse where the Bengali has kalā, and adds fur (spu). Rāhu is kept out of the English line.

lines.gloss: in the sky · having risen · grazes, feeds · amaṇa (aman rice? mindless?) · paddy, grain (?)
lines.en: rising into the [sky]{gagana}, it grazes on [amaṇa dhāṇa]{amana-dhana}.

flags.note: amaṇa dhāṇa is kept in source form, as the glossary's policy requires. dhāṇa is probably 'paddy, grain' (Sanskrit dhānya); amaṇa may be the aman rice crop or a-manas, 'mindless', perhaps both at once. The Tibetan has yid kyi chos, 'the mind's dharma'; Munidatta's paraphrase has the honey of ultimate bodhicitta in its place (cp.21.m4).

The Tibetan line, nam mkha' rkang pas 'gro zhing yid kyi chos, 'goes on foot in the sky, and the mind's dharma', has walking where the Bengali has rising (uṭhi) and grazing (caraa), and no verb for the last phrase.

lines.gloss: till then (so long), that (taba se) · mouse · leaping up · and about (jingle)
lines.en: Till then that [mouse]{mouse} leaps up and down;

flags.note: tabase is read as taba se, 'till then (so long), that [mouse]', looking forward to the teaching of 5b, as Munidatta's paraphrase supplies 'only so long as ... until' (tāvad eva ... yāvat) (cp.21.m5). The Tibetan has de tshe, 'then, at that time', which would give 'Then that mouse leaps up and down'.

uñcala pāñcala is taken as a jingling pair, 'leaping up and about' (compare Sanskrit ucchal-, 'leap up'); the Tibetan has mchong zhing rab tu 'gro, 'jumps and rushes about'. Munidatta's 'puffed up (unnata) with delusion and pride' (cp.21.m5) paraphrases it.

lines.gloss: true guru · by the teaching, making known (bodha) · make! · it, that one · still, motionless
lines.en: by the true [guru]{guru}'s teaching, make it still.

flags.note: bohe is taken as the instrumental of boha (Sanskrit bodha, 'awakening, making known'): 'by the teaching'. The Tibetan has gsung gis, 'by the word', and Munidatta speaks of 'the device of the true guru's word' (sadguruvacanayantra) (cp.21.m5).

lines.gloss: when · mouse · of (genitive ending; or: of this) · movement, roaming (cāra?) · breaks off, is cut off
lines.en: When the [mouse]{mouse}'s roaming is cut off,

flags.note: era is taken as the genitive ending of muṣā ('the mouse's'), and cā as a short form of cāra, 'movement, roaming' (compare cārā in 1a), as Munidatta's ācāra and the Tibetan comment's rgyu ba, 'moving', take it (cp.21.m6). era could also be 'of this'.
The Tibetan line has a leg instead of the roaming: gang du byi ba 'di yi rkang pa bcad byas na, 'when the leg of this mouse is cut'.

lines.gloss: Bhusuku · says · then · bond(s) · bursts, breaks

flags.note: The poet names himself Bhusuku; the glossary entry's English is Bhusukupāda, with the honorific. The line's own form (keep-source) is used, marked with p-bhusuku.
The Tibetan reads de tshe bcings grol b+hU su ku la smra, 'then the bonds are released, Bhusuku says'.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung. Varāḍī is probably the rāga that Sanskrit music treatises call Varāṭī. The Tibetan translation transcribes the name (ba rA DI).

The attribution 'of Bhusukupāda' (bhusukupādānām) stands before the song in the manuscript; Shastri's text runs it into line 1a. The Tibetan heading assigns the song, in the melody ba rA DI, to 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, apparently a rendering of the poet's name by meaning ('he of the three notions'); the last line of the Tibetan transcribes the name (b+hU su ku).

The song follows a house mouse through the night: it roams in the dark, eats, digs, ruins the stores and leaps about, and the refrain tells the yogi to kill it. Munidatta says Bhusukupāda sets out 'that same meaning' in the twilight language of 'mouse' (cp.21.m1), and derives mūṣaka, 'mouse', from muṣṇāti, 'steals' (cp.21.m2).

Shastri prints ধ্রু, the cue to sing the refrain, after couplet 1 as well as after the refrain and the later couplets. The refrain is couplet 2: Munidatta calls couplet 3 his 'second pada' (cp.21.m3) and couplet 6 his 'fifth' (cp.21.m6).

Shastri queries the word susāra. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads mtshan mo mun par byi ba rgyu byed cing, 'in the dark night the mouse roams, and', and this translation follows it by reading musāra, 'the mouse's', for susāra, a small change of one letter. Munidatta quotes only the opening words, niśi āndhīrī, and does not comment on the word (cp.21.m2).

Munidatta reads the mouse, 'the stealer', in twilight language as the mind-wind (cittapavana), and the night as wisdom (prajñā) or the action-woman (karmāṅganā). In the union of vajra and lotus, in the moments beginning with vicitra and through the joys beginning with the joy of the body, the mind-wind itself makes its meal of the taste of the nectar of bodhicitta (cp.21.m2). The Tibetan comment has 'mind and wind' and makes the night 'the limb of the wisdom action seal'.

On the refrain Munidatta says that, by the means received from the glorious guru's mouth, it is swiftly made without intrinsic nature, and that for the novice yogin (bālayogin) coming and going in the wheel of saṃsāra is not cut off and the mind does not shine (cp.21.m2). The Tibetan comment has the novice, separated from that means, make the mind suffer.

The Tibetan refrain has negatives the Bengali lacks: kye'i rnal 'byor rlung byi ma bsad cing / gang gis 'gro dang 'ong ba ma bkag na, 'O yogin, not killing the wind-mouse, if coming and going is not stopped by it'. It turns the command into a warning, and makes one compound, 'wind-mouse' (rlung byi), of the Bengali 'mouse, wind'.

Munidatta says the second pada describes the behaviour of the mind-mouse. Taking bhava as 'what comes into being' (bhavati), he says the mouse tears apart existence, one's own body, through its natural restlessness, and itself brings about the fall into the bad destinies, the animal realm, the hells and the rest; knowing this natural fault, the yogin, by the instruction won through grace, is not to impute real existence to it (cp.21.m3).

gātī is most likely 'hole, pit' (compare Sanskrit garta). Munidatta cites it as gatī and takes it as gati, 'destiny' (cp.21.m3). The Tibetan line has the mouse bore through a wall (rtsig pa 'bugs), and the Tibetan comment makes the wall the fall into the bad destinies (ngan 'gro).

Two words in this line are uncertain. kaliām̐ is taken here as 'having looked over', from kal-, 'observe, reckon': Munidatta's comment on the couplet has ākalayya, 'having reckoned', and the Tibetan comment bgrangs nas, 'having counted', though he applies it to the yogin, who is to reckon the mouse's natural fault (cp.21.m3). thātī is taken as 'store, what is laid by'; the Tibetan line has snod rnams, 'vessels'.

kalā can be 'black' (kāla), as the Tibetan comment takes it when it quotes the word as nag po, and kāla is also 'time, death', the destroyer: Munidatta says the mind-mouse is kāla because it destroys conventional bodhicitta (cp.21.m4). The Tibetan comment glosses the word as Rāhu (sgra gcan), who destroys the moon of conventional bodhicitta, and its version of the line puts Rāhu into the verse: byi ba sgra gcan spu dang kha dog med, 'the mouse, Rāhu, has no fur and no colour'.

'Has no colour' follows Munidatta, who reads bāṇa as varṇa, 'colour': when the mouse is examined through piṇḍagrāha and anubheda, he says, there is no instruction for apprehending colour (cp.21.m4); and the Tibetan line has kha dog med, 'without colour'. How uhaṇa comes to mean 'lacking' is not clear.

amaṇa dhāṇa: what the mouse grazes on in the sky; the sense is uncertain. dhāṇa is probably 'paddy, grain' (Sanskrit dhānya), and amaṇa may name the aman, a rice crop of Bengal, or be a-manas, 'mindless'; the phrase may play on both. The Tibetan has yid kyi chos, 'the mind's dharma'.

Munidatta explains 'sky' with a paraphrase: through the guru's lineage the mouse goes to the lotus grove of great bliss, comes back, and tastes the drinking of the honey of ultimate bodhicitta. He puts this where the song has it graze amaṇa dhāṇa, without an explicit gloss, and then quotes an Old Bengali verse of Mīnanātha 'in another school', in which the guru tells of the road of the ultimate and the bee drinks the honey of the opened lotus (cp.21.m4).

Munidatta says this couplet, his third pada, tells the greatness of the vajra guru: the mind-mouse stays puffed up with delusion and pride only until the device of the true guru's word is at hand, so the yogin should set his aspiration on the guru; he cites Saraha's verse beginning 'by the rays of whose grace' (cp.21.m5).

tabase is read as taba se, 'till then, that [mouse]', looking forward to 5b; Munidatta's paraphrase supplies 'only so long as ... until' (cp.21.m5), while the Tibetan has de tshe, 'then'. uñcala pāñcala is a jingling pair, 'leaping up and about'.

cā is taken as a short form of cāra, 'movement, roaming', as Munidatta's ācāra and the Tibetan comment's rgyu ba, 'moving', take it (cp.21.m6). The Tibetan line instead has the mouse's leg cut: gang du byi ba 'di yi rkang pa bcad byas na, 'when the leg of this mouse is cut'.

Munidatta's comment, whose syntax is loose, speaks of the movement of the mind-mouse in innate joy and of the imputation 'I' being cut off; at that time, he says, its bond of saṃsāra bursts (sphiṭa). He quotes a verse: saṃsāra does not exist in reality for the embodied, so what bondage is there; the confusion of taking a rope for a snake or a shadow for a ghost is made by false imputation; give up nothing, grasp nothing, but play, abiding in yourself as you are (cp.21.m6).
The Tibetan reads de tshe bcings grol b+hU su ku la smra, 'then the bonds are released, Bhusuku says'.

termsOmitted.reason: kalā (not among the detected hits) is rendered 'black', not the glossary's 'Death'; Munidatta's kāla reading is given in the notes and flagged for the reviewer.
Rāhu (sgra gcan) is only in the Tibetan line, which puts the commentary's gloss into the verse; the Bengali does not have it, and the mouse entry bars 'Rāhu' from the verse line.
Only in the Tibetan (yid kyi chos, 'the mind's dharma') for amaṇa dhāṇa; the Bengali word is kept as amaṇa dhāṇa.
The Tibetan rkang pa here means 'foot' (rkang pas 'gro, 'goes on foot'), not 'verse'; nothing in the Bengali line.
The Tibetan rkang pa here means 'leg' (the mouse's leg is cut), not 'verse'; nothing in the Bengali line.

questions: 1a: I emended susāra to musāra, 'the mouse's', on the evidence of the Tibetan (byi ba rgyu byed, 'the mouse roams'), and rendered 'the mouse goes roaming'. Accept the emendation, or keep susāra as an unexplained word (and if so, how should the line read)?

4a: I rendered kalā as 'black' (the Tibetan comment's nag po; the dark night of 1a; the paradox with 'no colour') and left Munidatta's kāla, the destroyer of conventional bodhicitta (cp.21.m4), to the notes. Confirm, or use the glossary's 'Death' (kala)? Either way, should the kala entry gain কলা as a form and 'black' as a variant, since the word has both senses?
4a: 'has no colour' for uhaṇa bāṇa rests on Munidatta's varṇa and the Tibetan kha dog med; uhaṇa as 'lacking' is my guess. Is this acceptable?

3b: 'looks over the stores and destroys them' is tentative for kaliām̐ nāśaka thātī (kal-, 'reckon', after Munidatta's ākalayya). Would you prefer 'wreaks ruin on the stores' (kar- with l for r) or another reading?
2a: musā pabaṇā as apposition, 'the mouse, the wind'. Would you rather follow the Tibetan compound, 'the wind-mouse', or read 'the mouse and the wind'?
5a: tabase as 'till then' (looking forward to the guru's teaching, as Munidatta's tāvat ... yāvat), or 'then' (the Tibetan de tshe)?

6b and heading: the bhaṇitā has the line's own form 'Bhusuku' marked with p-bhusuku, whose English is 'Bhusukupāda'; should 'Bhusuku' be added as a variant? And is it right to name the poet in the heading from the attribution bhusukupādānām that stands before the song?
4b: amaṇa dhāṇa is kept in source form by policy. If the aman-rice reading is accepted, would you prefer a translation such as 'aman grain'?
